stories.headline: California prosecutors slam Newsom's death row commutations, accuse governor of putting 'politics over people'
stories.note: Newsom's own state's prosecutors are hammering him on crime, a gift to any 2028 opponent.
body: Gov. Gavin Newsom has commuted the sentences of all 548 inmates on California's death row, converting them to life in prison without parole. District attorneys and police unions around the state responded with sharp public criticism.

Newsom explained the move in an open letter, arguing that state executions clash with California's values. He has kept an executive moratorium on capital punishment in place since taking office in 2019, and the state hasn't executed anyone since 2006.

San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow said victims' families weren't consulted or even notified before the announcement, and called the decision "all about politics." Los Angeles County DA Nathan Hochman pointed out that California voters have twice rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty.

Orange County DA Todd Spitzer and Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco also blasted the blanket clemency. Bianco said 127 of the inmates were sentenced for crimes committed in his county after full trials and jury decisions. The commuted cases include men convicted of murdering a toddler and two college students.

Anti-death-penalty advocates praised the governor, arguing the system is flawed and racially biased. Dow countered that California's defense procedures are rigorous and that he has confidence in the convictions.

Why it matters: Newsom is widely seen as a 2028 Democratic contender, and overriding voters and juries on the worst killers gives Republicans a vivid soft-on-crime contrast, voiced by his own state's prosecutors.

stories.headline: GOP eyes Senate comeback after Democratic bloodbath, but another political nightmare could await
stories.note: Republicans already see a realistic path to retake the Senate in 2028.
body: After Tuesday's Democratic sweep, Republicans are already mapping a route back to a Senate majority, possibly as soon as 2028. Democrats and the independents who caucus with them hold at least 54 seats, with Mississippi and Alaska still uncalled.

If Republicans keep the vice presidency, they'd need to flip at least four seats in 2028. Democrats will be defending seats in New Hampshire, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio that cycle, while the GOP must protect Wisconsin, Iowa and North Carolina.

There are risks. Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley turned 93 in September, and Democrats could try to add Puerto Rico and D.C. as states, though that would likely require ending the filibuster and getting past a likely Trump veto.

Heritage Action's Chip Wyatt said a GOP night like the Democrats just had is "feasible" if conservatives focus on affordability while Democrats let their fringe set the agenda. Sen. Ted Cruz said Republicans will be ready "when the zealots overreach."
Looking further ahead, the 2032 map repeats this year's races, giving the GOP another shot at deep-red states like Kansas and South Carolina that sent Democrats to the Senate this year.
Why it matters: The loss was big, but the next map gives Republicans real targets, and two years is a long time in politics.

stories.headline: 4 of nation's largest cities now led by socialist mayors after Tuesday's election, affecting tens of millions
stories.note: Socialist mayors running four huge cities hands the GOP a ready-made message about the Democratic Party's direction.
body: Tuesday's elections put socialist mayors in charge of Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., meaning four of America's 20 largest cities are now run by Democratic Socialists of America members.

In Los Angeles, Councilwoman Nithya Raman beat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass and takes office in December. In D.C., Janeese Lewis George cruised to victory. They join Seattle's Katie Wilson and New York City's Zohran Mamdani.
Those four cities are home to about 14 million people, and roughly 44 million when their metro areas are counted, since crime, housing and business conditions in a city spill into nearby suburbs.

Voters also sent seven DSA-backed or affiliated candidates to the House, including members from New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado, Michigan and California. Heritage Foundation fellow Mike Gonzalez warned that Marxists who "took over universities" are now taking over city halls.
Polling shows socialism still trails capitalism: a Fox News poll found 32% of voters view socialism favorably versus 51% for capitalism, though socialism's favorability matches a record high.
Why it matters: With socialists running America's biggest cities, Republicans will have real-world results to point to as they argue the Democratic Party has moved far left.

stories.headline: Democrat who toppled GOP incumbent will head to court on felony charge just days after election upset
stories.note: One of the Democrats' new winners is starting the job facing a felony charge.
body: Democrat LaKesha Womack, who narrowly defeated Republican Rep. Tim Moore in North Carolina's 14th District, is due in court on Nov. 10 on a pending felony charge.

She won 51.1% to 48.9%, according to AP results. The charge alleges she failed to return a rental car worth about $20,000 in 2019. The summons was issued in January 2020 but wasn't served until October 2026.

Womack has acknowledged returning the car late, saying she was homeless at the time and didn't know a criminal case had been filed. She declined to comment on the charge Friday, though she issued a statement calling her win historic.

The offense is a Class H felony in North Carolina that can carry more than two years in prison depending on criminal history. Under House rules, members charged with such a felony are expected to step aside from committee and leadership posts while the case is pending.
Before the election, Moore said his opponent needed to explain the charge to voters, noting the court date fell the week after Election Day.
Why it matters: One of the Democrats' surprise pickups starts her term under a legal cloud, which could limit her role in the House and keeps the seat in play for 2028.

stories.headline: Dems pivot from ‘affordability’ pitch to DHS probe threats after midterm wins
stories.note: Democrats are already trading their cost-of-living pitch for investigations, an easy bait-and-switch attack for Republicans.
body: Several Democrats who campaigned on lowering costs turned almost immediately to promising investigations of the Trump administration after their midterm wins, especially its immigration enforcement.

Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead House Oversight, posted "Lawyer Up" on election night. Rep. Delia Ramirez told Noem, Homan, Miller and others to "clear your schedule," Rep. Analilia Mejia promised subpoenas "like Mardi Gras beads," and Rep. Yassamin Ansari promised subpoenas in January and called for Hegseth's impeachment.

Sen. Ed Markey, who listed groceries and gas prices as priorities, joked about the forests needed for all the subpoenas. Most of these lawmakers didn't respond to Fox News Digital; Garcia's office pointed to a later post tying corruption to affordability.

DHS's top lawyer called it "political shenanigans," and the Justice Department said it isn't afraid of Democrats' threats. The White House said Trump is still willing to work with Democrats on issues that help working Americans.

Former immigration judge Andrew Arthur said Congress has every right to investigate DHS, but noted that much of the administration's enforcement rests on laws Congress itself passed and that going after Tom Homan may not be popular.
Why it matters: Democrats won on affordability and are already talking mostly about subpoenas, an easy bait-and-switch message for Republicans heading into 2028.

stories.headline: American war hero details dire living conditions US troops face as Hegseth taps him to 'fix' it
stories.note: Hegseth is putting a decorated veteran in charge of fixing troops' housing, a strong pro-military story.
body: Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer, now senior adviser to the Pentagon's Barracks Task Force, says War Secretary Pete Hegseth has tasked him with fixing military barracks after decades of neglect.

Meyer has toured more than eight Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine installations and plans to visit 30 by year's end. He described troops going a year without hot water, sleeping in cars to escape barracks with no air conditioning, and living with mold and water damage.

A 2023 GAO report documented serious hazards, and 12 of its 31 recommendations remain open. Billions have been committed under past efforts, but problems persist, and a separate review found a $285 billion maintenance backlog.

Meyer said Hegseth gave the task force real authority to direct money and decisions, and told him plainly, "He expects me to fix it." He blamed red tape, contracting rules and Congress's failure to pass a full-year defense budget, not just funding levels.

He criticized prior Pentagon leadership for not making barracks a priority, while saying many commanders want to help but lack the tools. His goal is housing he would be fine with his own daughters living in.
Why it matters: Hegseth putting a decorated war hero in charge of troops' basic living conditions is a strong, concrete pro-military story for the administration.

stories.headline: US offers $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear program
stories.note: The administration keeps up the pressure on Iran's nuclear program.
body: The State Department's Rewards for Justice program is offering up to $20 million for information on Iran's nuclear program, including its scientists, technologies, facilities and related organizations.

Tipsters can reach the program through Signal or a Tor-based tip line and may qualify for relocation as well as a reward. The department said it remains committed to countering any Iranian attempt to build a nuclear weapon.

The offer comes as President Trump weighs renewed military strikes on Iran while talks with Tehran continue. Trump met with his national security team Thursday after promising to wait until after the midterms to decide.
Trump reiterated Friday that Iran will never get a nuclear weapon. "You'll know soon enough," he told reporters about a possible decision.
U.S. officials noted that Nov. 9 brings a new moon in the Middle East, favorable for military operations, and Central Command is reportedly finalizing plans though it hasn't received a new directive.
Why it matters: Even after the midterm losses, the administration is keeping maximum pressure on Iran, a national-security strength Republicans can point to.
